The image below shows the $x^x$-spindle, as [described by Mark Meyerson](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2691469){target=_blank}.

::: {style="max-width: 800px; margin-inline: auto"} 
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {make_spindle} from './components/make_spindle.js'

viewof n = Inputs.range([0, 15], {
  value: 15,
  step: 1,
  label: "Thread pairs"
})

spindle = {
  const plot = make_spindle();
  invalidation.then(() => plot.destroy());
  return plot;
}
```
:::

## Explanation

For real $x$, $f(x) = x^x$ can be viewed as a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$. In fact, there are infinitely many such functions given by the various branches. To see this, let's write
$$
x^x = e^{x\log(x)}.
$$
Now, the complex log has many branches defined by
$$
\log(x) = \ln(|x|) + i(\text{Arg}(x) + 2k\pi).
$$
Each choice of $k$ yields a new branch. Those separate branches are illustrated by the separate threads in the plot.


```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
spindle.update(n)
```

## Crossing the real plane

In a calculus class, it's common to define 
$$x^{p/q} = (\sqrt[q]{x})^p.$$
In this definition, we're assuming that $p$ is an integer and $q$ is a positive, even integer.  Thus, when $x$ is negative, $x^{p/q}$ is

- well defined and positive, when $p$ is even,
- well defined and negative, when $p$ is odd, and
- not defined otherwise.

We can plot this graph for our calculus students like so:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {real_intersection_plot} from './components/real_intersections.js'
real_intersection_plot(15, {width: Math.min(width, 800)})
```

As is often the case, the more complete view of complex variables sheds like on the real viewpoint. Indeed, the dots occur where one of the threads puncture the $x$-$\text{Re}(x^x)$ plane. For negative $x$, in fact, branch $k$ has imaginary part
$$
|x|^x\sin\!\bigl(\pi x(2k+1)\bigr).
$$
Thus the crossings occur exactly when $x(2k+1)$ is an integer.
